title: Microsoft's November Patch Tuesday ships 1,094 fixes, including an Outlook zero-day
dek: Microsoft's November 2026 update fixes more than 1,000 flaws. One Outlook bug was already being used to steal Windows login hashes. Here's what to patch first.
body:
Microsoft released its November security updates on November 10, and for the second month in a row the total topped 1,000. Counts differ slightly between trackers depending on what they include, but most put the figure near 1,094, with 63 flaws rated critical.
## The one already under attack
Only one bug, CVE-2026-124194, was being exploited before the fix arrived. It is an Outlook spoofing flaw that Microsoft rates only "Moderate" (CVSS 6.5), but it matters because it can leak a user's NTLMv2 password hash. Attackers can try to crack that hash or relay it to sign in elsewhere as the victim. The root cause is that Outlook failed to warn the user about an unsafe action.
CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list the same day and gave federal agencies until November 24 to patch.
## Other fixes worth noticing
Researchers flagged several critical remote code execution bugs, including a Windows LDAP flaw that can hit domain controllers and a Windows Search bug that is reachable through Exchange Server. That means Exchange servers need the Windows update as well as their Exchange patches.
## Watch out for this
The Outlook fix ships through Microsoft 365 Apps and Office updates, not the Windows cumulative update. Installing Windows updates alone does not close the hole.
who: Windows and Office users, especially anyone using Outlook, plus IT teams running Exchange, SharePoint and Windows servers.
todo: Run Windows Update and Office updates now. IT teams should patch Outlook first, then domain controllers and internet-facing servers.

title: Chrome patches its eighth actively exploited zero-day of the year
dek: Google fixed CVE-2026-125350, an XML memory bug attackers were already exploiting. It is Chrome's eighth zero-day of 2026. Restart your browser to apply it.
body:
Google released Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux, fixing nine security bugs. One of them, CVE-2026-125350, is a use-after-free flaw in Chrome's XML handling, and Google says an exploit for it exists in the wild.
That makes it the eighth Chrome zero-day patched in 2026. CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 10.
## What we know about the attacks
As usual with Chrome zero-days, Google has not said who is using the bug or against whom. Researchers note the flaw could allow code to run inside Chrome's sandbox. No public report has confirmed that the exploit also escapes the sandbox to take over the computer.
## Why restarting matters
Chrome downloads updates on its own, but a fix doesn't take effect until the browser restarts. Many people leave Chrome open for days, so their browser stays vulnerable even after the patch has downloaded.
who: Anyone using Google Chrome on Windows, Mac or Linux.
todo: Open Chrome's menu, go to Help > About Google Chrome to fetch the update, then restart the browser.

title: Firefox 160 fixes 99 security flaws
dek: Mozilla's November 10 releases patch 99 vulnerabilities in Firefox 160, with matching fixes for the extended support release and Thunderbird.
body:
Mozilla shipped Firefox 160 on November 10, the same day as Microsoft's Patch Tuesday. The release fixes 99 security vulnerabilities, 57 of them rated high.
Firefox ESR 153.7, the extended support release that many businesses use, fixes 81 vulnerabilities. Thunderbird 160 and Thunderbird 153.7 carry the shared fixes as well, including a flaw involving privilege escalation and sandbox escape.
No Firefox flaw in this batch was reported as exploited. Browser bugs of this kind are a favorite target once details become public, though, so it's worth installing the update rather than waiting for the next restart.
who: Firefox and Thunderbird users, including organizations on the extended support release.
todo: Update to Firefox 160 (or ESR 153.7) and Thunderbird 160 or 153.7, then restart them.

title: N-able pulls N-central cloud offline after 33 zero-days go public
dek: A researcher published exploit code for 33 alleged flaws in N-able's N-central remote management tool. N-able took its hosted service offline and shipped hotfixes.
body:
Late on Sunday, November 8, a researcher posted details and proof-of-concept code for 33 alleged vulnerabilities in N-central to a GitHub repository called "Able2Shell." N-central is a remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform that IT service providers use to run their customers' computers and servers.
The researcher says the flaws chain into attacks that can steal credentials, create an administrator account and run commands as root, some without logging in. He told reporters he went public without warning N-able because the company had allegedly failed to fix bugs he reported earlier.
## N-able's response
On November 9, N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline across the Americas, Europe and Asia-Pacific. It told customers who run N-central on their own servers to shut them down too. It then released N-central 2026.4 HF2, which patches what it called the most critical issues. The hotfix lists seven CVEs.
N-able initially said it had seen no exploitation. Security firms soon reported probing of N-central servers for the newly published flaws.
## Why it matters
A compromised RMM server can be a master key to every customer it manages, which is why attackers prize these tools.
who: Managed service providers and IT teams that use N-able N-central to run their clients' computers.
todo: Apply N-able's hotfixes as they arrive, and watch the vendor's status page before turning cloud access back on.

title: CISA flags four exploited flaws in OpenSSH, FreeSWITCH, GPUStack and IBM Aspera
dek: CISA added four actively exploited flaws to its must-patch list on November 9 and gave federal agencies three days to fix them.
body:
On Monday, November 9, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. That listing means CISA has evidence attackers are using them. Federal civilian agencies had until November 12 to patch.
## The four flaws
- GPUStack (CVE-2026-102895): an authentication flaw in a tool for managing GPU clusters and serving AI models. Fixed in version 2.2.0. Recorded attacks included creating malicious backends.
- FreeSWITCH (CVE-2026-116779): a code injection bug, CVSS 9.8, in the open-source phone switch behind many VoIP systems. A crafted SIP message could run FreeSWITCH commands. Fixed in 1.11.3.
- OpenSSH (CVE-2026-123158): a login bypass nicknamed "SSHole" that affects only certain musl-based Linux builds without PAM, such as older Alpine Linux. Fixed in OpenSSH 10.6p2.
- IBM Aspera Faspex (CVE-2026-123218): an authorization bypass, CVSS 9.8, that can lead to full administrator access on the file-transfer platform. Fixed in 5.0.19 PL1.
## Patching isn't the end
CISA asked agencies to do forensic checks too. An attacker who got in before the patch may have created accounts or credentials that keep working afterward.
who: Organizations running GPUStack, FreeSWITCH phone systems, IBM Aspera Faspex or some Linux builds of OpenSSH.
todo: Patch to the fixed versions, then look for new admin accounts or credentials an attacker may have added.

title: Attackers probe an OpenSSH login bypass on some Linux builds
dek: Exploitation attempts have begun against "SSHole," an OpenSSH login bypass that affects certain musl-based Linux builds without PAM. OpenSSH 10.6p2 fixes it.
body:
OpenSSH runs on millions of servers, so any login flaw in it gets attention fast. This one, tracked as CVE-2026-123158 and nicknamed "SSHole," is narrower than it sounds. It affects OpenSSH builds before 10.6p2 on Linux systems that use the musl C library and don't use PAM for authentication. Alpine Linux before 3.24.4, popular in containers, is the main example.
Researchers have recorded exploitation attempts from 13 IP addresses in nine countries. That is an early sign of scanning that often comes before wider attacks. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list on November 9.
## Am I affected?
Most mainstream Linux servers, which use glibc and PAM, are not affected. Security teams are advised to check their distribution, OpenSSH version and authentication setup instead of assuming every OpenSSH install is exposed.
who: Servers running certain musl-based Linux builds of OpenSSH without PAM, common in Alpine-style containers.
todo: Update to OpenSSH 10.6p2 or your distribution's patched package, and limit SSH access to trusted networks.

title: SonicWall fixes seven SonicOS flaws, one already under attack
dek: SonicWall patched seven SonicOS firewall flaws. One, CVE-2026-19868, can skip SAML sign-in and multi-factor login on the SSL VPN and is already being exploited.
body:
On Friday, November 6, SonicWall published an advisory covering seven vulnerabilities in SonicOS, the operating system on its firewalls and virtual NSv appliances.
## The exploited one
CVE-2026-19868 is rated 7.1, lower than two of the other bugs. It is the dangerous one anyway. It lets an attacker who holds valid credentials for an alternate login method get around SAML authentication on the SSL VPN, and with it any multi-factor authentication enforced through SAML. SonicWall said it had investigated a report of exploitation. CISA added the flaw to its must-patch list the same day and set a November 20 deadline for federal agencies.
There is no workaround. Fixed releases are SonicOS 7.3.4-7013 or later for Gen7 devices and 8.2.3-8015 or later for Gen8.
## The other six
The rest include two management-interface flaws rated 8.8 and a pre-authentication memory bug. None were reported as exploited, but they're fixed in the same update.
who: Businesses with SonicWall firewalls that use SSL VPN or multi-factor login.
todo: Install SonicWall's SonicOS update and review VPN logins for anything unusual. U.S. federal agencies must patch by Nov 20.

title: Zyxel switch hacks turn out to be a zero-day, not an old bug
dek: Attacks that compromised about 1,000 Zyxel GS1900 switches used a previously unknown flaw, not the one Zyxel patched in June. New firmware fixes it.
body:
In September, threat intelligence firm GreyNoise reported that a suspected Chinese-speaking hacker had compromised close to 1,000 Zyxel GS1900 network switches, and blamed CVE-2026-7273. Zyxel had already patched that bug in June, so the attacks looked like a case of slow patching.
Firmware security firm Binarly found something different. The exploit used in the intrusions still worked on switches that had the June fix, because it abused a separate, unknown flaw in the same code. That flaw is now tracked as CVE-2026-107441, an out-of-bounds write that lets an attacker run operating system commands without logging in.
Binarly says 996 switches in 48 countries were compromised, with configuration files, network details and hashed root credentials exposed. Zyxel has not confirmed that count.
## The fix
Binarly reported the flaw to Zyxel on September 29. Zyxel released "Patch 3" firmware for ten GS1900 models in October and published its advisory on November 3. Switches that were patched in June and marked as done still need this update.
who: Owners of Zyxel GS1900 network switches, often found in small offices.
todo: Install Zyxel's latest firmware and keep the switch's admin page off the internet.

title: Quest Foglight for Databases hit with eight critical bugs
dek: The Zero Day Initiative disclosed eight serious flaws in Quest Foglight for Databases, six allowing remote code execution and two privilege escalation.
body:
On November 3, Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative published advisories for eight vulnerabilities in Quest Foglight for Databases, a tool companies use to monitor database performance.
Six of the flaws could let an attacker run code on the Foglight server remotely. The other two allow privilege escalation, giving an attacker who already has a foothold more control.
No exploitation was reported at the time of disclosure. Monitoring servers are attractive targets, though, because they usually hold credentials and connections to the databases they watch. Quest customers should apply the vendor's updates and keep Foglight reachable only from inside their network.
who: Companies that use Quest Foglight to monitor their databases.
todo: Apply Quest's updates and make sure the Foglight server is only reachable from inside your network.

title: Android's November update patches 216 vulnerabilities
dek: Google's November 2026 Android security bulletin fixes 216 flaws, 23 of them critical. None were marked as exploited. Look for patch level 2026-11-05.
body:
Google's Android security bulletin for November 2026 fixes 216 vulnerabilities, one of the largest monthly bulletins in recent memory. Twenty-three are rated critical. Google did not mark any of them as exploited in the wild.
The fixes reach phones as security patch level 2026-11-05 or later. Pixel phones usually get them first. Samsung, Motorola and other makers roll them out on their own schedules, sometimes weeks later.
## How to check
Open Settings and look for the security update or security patch level, usually under About phone or Security. If your device no longer gets monthly patches, it may be time to plan a replacement.
who: Android phone and tablet owners.
todo: Go to Settings > Security and install the update. Look for patch level 2026-11-05 or later once your phone maker releases it.

title: Russia's Turla uses new Cereal malware to steal government email
dek: ESET found Cereal, a stealthy new Turla toolkit, inside government Exchange servers in Kazakhstan and Romania, copying emails tied to NATO and the EU.
body:
Researchers at ESET have documented a new espionage toolkit they call Cereal, named for its heavy use of serialization. They attribute it with high confidence to Turla, the Russia-aligned group also known as Snake and widely linked to Russia's FSB.
## Where it was found
ESET found Cereal on Microsoft Exchange servers at two national government organizations, one in Kazakhstan and one in Romania. In the Romanian case, the malware was set to pick out emails sent to or from NATO and European Union addresses.
## How it hides
Cereal is a modular .NET toolkit with eight connected parts. Its email-collecting component, CerealBox, works inside Exchange's own mail transport process and copies messages that have Word or PDF attachments and match chosen senders, recipients or subjects. Mail keeps flowing normally. Another component takes commands through web requests that look like ordinary Exchange traffic, so the server never calls out to an attacker's machine. That defeats a common way of spotting infections.
ESET's research doesn't say how Turla first got onto the servers. Turla has targeted Exchange since at least 2014.
who: Government agencies and organizations running their own Microsoft Exchange email servers.
todo: Keep Exchange fully patched and watch for unusual mailbox access or new server-side tools.

title: Bitter hackers deploy a new PapRAT backdoor across South Asia
dek: The Bitter espionage group is using a newly documented remote access tool, PapRAT, in a campaign aimed at targets in South Asia.
body:
Security researchers have documented a new backdoor, PapRAT, being used by the long-running espionage group known as Bitter in a campaign aimed at South Asia.
Bitter, also tracked as T-APT-17, has historically gone after government, military and energy organizations in the region. Its campaigns usually start with spear-phishing emails carrying malicious attachments.
A remote access trojan like PapRAT lets the operators control an infected computer, steal files and run further tools. Organizations in the region should treat unexpected attachments with suspicion and keep endpoint protection up to date.
who: Government, military and other organizations in South Asia.
todo: Be wary of unexpected email attachments, and keep endpoint security tools up to date.

title: China-aligned spies hijack Sogou keyboard updates to plant DarkVigil
dek: A China-aligned espionage group abused the update traffic of Sogou Input Method, a popular Chinese typing app, to install DarkVigil spyware.
body:
Researchers report that a China-aligned espionage group hijacked the update process of Sogou Input Method, one of China's most widely used keyboard apps, to install spyware called DarkVigil.
Software updates are a powerful way in for attackers. Users and security tools tend to trust them, and an app like an input method editor sees everything the user types.
Anyone who uses Sogou should make sure it's updated through official channels and run a security scan. Organizations should watch for unusual update traffic from endpoint software.
who: People using the Sogou Input Method keyboard app.
todo: Make sure Sogou is updated from its official source, and run a security scan if you use it.

title: APT29-linked group hijacks an analytics script to hit iPhones and Androids
dek: Sekoia links APT29 to a campaign that hijacked the Plerdy analytics script and fake sites to push exploits for already-patched iPhone and Android flaws.
body:
French security firm Sekoia published a report on November 4 that ties a mobile espionage campaign, with moderate to high confidence, to APT29. That is the group associated with Russia's foreign intelligence service, the SVR.
## How the attack worked
The attackers used three routes. They injected code into hacked websites, built lookalike copies of real sites, and compromised Plerdy, a Ukrainian web analytics service. From August 27 to September 3, 2026, Plerdy's tracking script, used by thousands of mostly Ukrainian websites, also delivered the attackers' profiling code to visitors.
That code checked each visitor's phone and browser version. If the device was vulnerable, it served a matching exploit chain. No tap or download was needed beyond loading the page. The payloads were built to steal browser cookies, messages and saved Wi-Fi passwords.
## The good news
The exploits targeted flaws that Apple and Google had already fixed, so they only worked against phones that hadn't been updated. Current iOS releases and up-to-date Chrome on Android postdate every version the campaign targeted.
who: iPhone and Android users who visited websites carrying the tampered analytics script, mainly espionage targets.
todo: Install the latest iOS and Android updates. People at higher risk can turn on Apple's Lockdown Mode.

title: China-linked hackers chain PHP2Shell bugs to take over Palo Alto firewalls
dek: A suspected China-nexus group chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel bug to root 25 Palo Alto Networks systems, including firewalls tied to a U.S. government-affiliated network.
body:
PHP2Shell is the nickname for two critical PHP flaws (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) that the PHP project fixed on October 21. Within days, attackers were using them.
On October 28, Palo Alto Networks confirmed active exploitation against PAN-OS firewalls whose management interface is exposed to the internet. The company says only about 0.02% of customers expose that interface.
## The campaign
Security firm Dream described a suspected China-nexus operation that used the FOFA search engine to find about 19,000 internet-facing Palo Alto firewalls. It then chained PHP2Shell with Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300), a Linux kernel privilege-escalation bug, to gain root access. The group rooted 25 systems, 24 perimeter firewalls and one internal management server, some belonging to a U.S. government-affiliated organization.
At that organization, the attackers set up a reverse SSH tunnel and moved to the internal server that manages every firewall, gaining access to all of their configurations and credentials. Researchers found traces of AI tools in the attack workflow. Palo Alto's Unit 42 independently verified the tooling.
## What to do
Apply Palo Alto's hotfixes. Where none exist yet, use its mitigations, and keep management interfaces off the internet.
who: Organizations with Palo Alto Networks firewalls whose management page is reachable from the internet.
todo: Patch the firewall, and never expose its management interface to the internet.

title: Cisco SD-WAN flaw used to plant malware that steals encryption keys
dek: Attackers exploited a Cisco SD-WAN flaw to plant malware that steals encryption keys. Cisco Talos linked the infrastructure to a known China-linked network.
body:
Attackers exploited a vulnerability in Cisco SD-WAN, the software many companies use to connect branch offices, to install malware designed to steal encryption keys.
Cisco Talos linked the malware's infrastructure to the "Silent Train" network that Lumen has tied to Volt Typhoon, a China-linked group known for targeting critical infrastructure.
Stolen keys can let attackers read or tamper with traffic between a company's sites. This incident adds to a run of exploited Cisco SD-WAN bugs this year. Administrators should apply Cisco's fixes and check SD-WAN management systems for configuration changes or software they don't recognize.
who: Companies that run Cisco SD-WAN to connect their offices.
todo: Apply Cisco's fixes and check SD-WAN management systems for changes you didn't make.

title: Vanderbilt University hit by the new BYOD ransomware gang
dek: Vanderbilt University was listed by BYOD, a ransomware gang that launched in 2026 and claims it stole university data.
body:
Vanderbilt University in Nashville has been named as a victim by BYOD, a ransomware group that first appeared in 2026. The gang claims it stole data from the university.
BYOD is a small operation so far. At the time of the report, its leak site listed five other organizations. Gangs like this typically steal data before encrypting systems, then threaten to publish it unless a ransom is paid.
Claims on leak sites aren't always accurate, and the scope of any data theft wasn't confirmed at the time of the report. Students, staff and others whose information Vanderbilt holds should watch for official notices. They should also be wary of phishing emails that mention the attack, a common follow-up tactic.
who: Vanderbilt students, staff and others whose data the university holds.
todo: Watch for a notice from Vanderbilt and be extra careful with emails that mention the attack.

title: Ransomware tracker: 35 German organizations on leak sites in a month
dek: A German tally counted 35 organizations with ties to Germany posted on extortion leak sites in the 30 days to November 4, with Qilin and The Gentlemen most active.
body:
A German situation report counted 35 organizations with ties to Germany that ransomware and extortion gangs posted on their leak sites in the 30 days up to November 4, 2026.
Qilin and The Gentlemen were among the most active groups. Both run "ransomware as a service" operations, renting their tools to affiliates who carry out the break-ins.
A leak-site listing is a claim, not proof, and the real number of attacks is usually higher because victims who pay quietly are never posted. Still, the count shows how steadily mid-sized German companies are being hit. Offline backups, fast patching of internet-facing systems and multi-factor login for remote access remain the best defenses.
who: Companies with operations in Germany, which gangs like Qilin and The Gentlemen are targeting.
todo: Keep offline backups, patch internet-facing systems quickly and require multi-factor login for remote access.

title: Cyberattack diverts ambulances at New Mexico's only Level 1 trauma center
dek: A cyberattack on UNM Health forced ambulances to be diverted from New Mexico's only Level 1 trauma center and disrupted classes at the University of New Mexico.
body:
A cyberattack on the University of New Mexico's Health Sciences Center disrupted UNM Hospital, New Mexico's only Level 1 trauma center, and ambulances had to be diverted elsewhere. Classes at the medical school and other UNM programs were cancelled while systems were down.
The Health Sciences Center covers UNM Hospital and the university's schools of medicine, pharmacy, nursing and population health. University officials said they would make no concessions to the hackers.
According to The Record, it is the second major cyberattack on a large state hospital system in 2026, after an attack shut down the University of Mississippi Medical Center's clinics in March. Patients should follow UNM Health's updates on appointments and watch for any notice about their data.
who: Patients and staff of UNM Health in New Mexico.
todo: Patients should follow UNM Health's updates for appointments and watch for any data breach notice.

title: Cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration force European stores to pull food
dek: Overnight on November 1–2, attackers tampered with refrigeration controls at supermarkets in at least seven European countries, forcing stores to throw out food.
body:
Overnight into Monday, November 2, refrigerators and freezers at supermarkets across Europe started warming up. Chains in Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Sweden, Ireland, Estonia and Finland reported problems, with later reports from Germany, Italy and Portugal. In some stores, units were switched into defrost mode or pushed as high as 50°C (122°F), and staff had to pull chilled and frozen food from sale.
Affected chains included Ahold Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg (around 40 locations), Coop and ICA in Sweden, and SuperValu in Ireland, which said 13 of its 223 stores were hit.
## Not ransomware, but sabotage
Nobody demanded payment. Attackers got remote access to refrigeration controllers and changed their settings, in many cases reportedly using factory-default passwords. It was the second wave in a month. In mid-October, controllers at hundreds of French supermarkets were tampered with, and France's cyber agency named refrigeration controller lines from Danfoss and Copeland.
SentinelLabs says Russian-aligned groups are credible suspects but that attribution remains open. The EU has said it will check supermarkets' readiness for such attacks.
who: Grocery chains in Europe that use connected refrigeration systems, and their shoppers.
todo: Retailers should separate building and refrigeration controls from the main network and the internet.

title: Abrigo shuts down Sageworks after suspicious activity, disrupting banks
dek: Abrigo took its Sageworks lending platform offline after detecting suspicious activity, disrupting U.S. banks and credit unions. Most services returned by November 2.
body:
Abrigo, a software provider for community banks and credit unions, shut down its Sageworks platform after detecting suspicious activity. Many U.S. lenders use Sageworks for loan processing and credit analysis.
The shutdown left banks and credit unions without access to the platform. Abrigo said most services were back by November 2, but some borrower-facing features stayed offline longer while the investigation continued.
The incident shows how one software vendor can become a single point of failure for hundreds of financial institutions. Borrowers with questions about loans in progress should contact their bank or credit union directly.
who: U.S. banks and credit unions that use Sageworks, and borrowers whose loans run through it.
todo: Borrowers with questions should contact their bank or credit union directly.

title: Ransomware claims jump 23% in the third quarter
dek: NCC Group counted 2,865 ransomware victim claims in Q3 2026, up 23% from the previous quarter, with industrial companies hit hardest.
body:
Ransomware activity climbed again in the third quarter of 2026. NCC Group's tracking counted 2,865 victims claimed on ransomware leak sites between July and September, up from 2,325 in the second quarter, a 23% rise.
Industrial companies were the most targeted sector. Attackers know that factory downtime is expensive, which raises the pressure to pay.
Leak-site counts undercount the real total, since victims who pay quickly are often never listed. The trend still shows ransomware growing despite police takedowns earlier in the year. Testing that backups can actually be restored, and patching internet-facing systems first, remain the most effective steps.
who: Organizations everywhere, with industrial companies hit hardest.
todo: Test that your backups can actually be restored, and patch internet-facing systems first.

title: Ransomware hits its fastest pace of 2026 despite the KillSec arrests
dek: Security vendors report ransomware attacks rising to their fastest pace of 2026 and more use of AI agents, even after police arrested KillSec suspects in September.
body:
Several security vendors report that ransomware attacks hit their fastest pace of the year this fall. The rise came even after police arrested suspected members of the KillSec group in late September.
Researchers also describe ransomware affiliates making more use of AI agents to scout targets, write phishing lures and speed up intrusions. That shortens the time defenders have to react.
Arrests and takedowns disrupt individual gangs, but affiliates often move to other groups quickly. Multi-factor login on every remote access point, offline backups and a rehearsed response plan matter more than any single law enforcement win.
who: Businesses of every size.
todo: Turn on multi-factor login everywhere, keep offline backups and rehearse your response plan.

title: Cirrus Aircraft discloses breach after a social engineering attack
dek: Cirrus Aircraft says a July social engineering attack exposed personal and health information. It notified Massachusetts and Texas regulators on November 10.
body:
Cirrus Aircraft, the Duluth, Minnesota maker of small planes and the Vision Jet, has disclosed a data breach caused by a social engineering attack on July 17, 2026. Social engineering means tricking an employee, for example with a phone call or message, rather than breaking in through a technical flaw.
The company says personal information and some health information were exposed. It reported the breach to regulators in Massachusetts and Texas on November 10.
People who receive a notice should read it closely and enroll in any credit or identity monitoring offered. Cases like this are a reminder that a convincing caller can do as much damage as malware.
who: People whose personal or health details Cirrus Aircraft holds, mainly customers and employees.
todo: Read any notice you receive and enroll in the free monitoring it offers.

title: Iris Ohyama cloud breach exposes data on 7.7 million customers
dek: A breach of a cloud service used by Japanese homeware maker Iris Ohyama exposed names, addresses and account passwords for about 7.7 million customers.
body:
Iris Ohyama, the Japanese maker of household goods and appliances, says a breach of a cloud service may have exposed the data of about 7.7 million customers of its online store, Iris Plaza.
According to the company's notice, the exposed information may include full names, physical addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, gender, dates of birth and account passwords. Credit card details were not stored in the affected service.
As of November 5, Iris Plaza said it had received no reports of misuse or financial loss. The exposure of passwords is the biggest worry. Anyone who used the same password elsewhere should change it on those sites too.
who: Customers of Iris Ohyama's online store, Iris Plaza.
todo: Change your Iris Plaza password and any other site where you used the same one.

title: Amplifon breach may affect 1.3 million U.S. hearing care customers
dek: A Texas filing shows the Amplifon hearing care data breach may affect about 1.33 million people, with health, insurance and ID details potentially exposed.
body:
Amplifon, one of the world's largest hearing aid and hearing care providers, has reported a data breach to the Texas attorney general that lists about 1.33 million affected people.
The files taken earlier this year may include health information, insurance details and government ID numbers, the kind of data that can be used for identity theft and insurance fraud.
Affected customers should read the mailed notice, enroll in any protection the company offers and check insurance statements for claims they don't recognize.
who: Amplifon hearing care customers in the U.S.
todo: Read your mailed notice, enroll in any protection offered and watch insurance statements for claims you don't recognize.

title: Chainalysis breached by attackers using AI agent techniques
dek: Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis says attackers used AI agent-driven methods to get into internal systems, exposing customer names.
body:
Chainalysis, the blockchain analytics company used by governments and crypto firms to trace funds, says attackers got into its internal systems. Customer names were exposed.
The company says the intruders used AI agent-driven techniques, automated tools that can explore systems and chain steps together far faster than a person working by hand. Reports of attackers using AI agents this way have become more common this year.
For customers, the main risk is targeted phishing. Emails that use your name and mention Chainalysis deserve extra suspicion.
who: Chainalysis customers.
todo: Watch for phishing emails that use your name or mention Chainalysis.

title: Applebee's app leaked customer data through a hardcoded database password
dek: A database password left inside the Applebee's app could let anyone who found it reach customers' personal information.
body:
The Applebee's app shipped with a database password written into its code. Anyone who pulled the app apart could find that password and use it to reach customers' personal information.
Hardcoded credentials are a well-known mistake. Apps are easy to download and inspect, so a secret placed inside one should be treated as public.
People with Applebee's accounts should change their password and watch for scam emails or texts that pose as the restaurant. Offers of free food or account problems are common lures.
who: People with accounts in the Applebee's app.
todo: Change your Applebee's password and watch for scam emails or texts posing as the restaurant.

title: DreamHost confirms attackers stole FTP logins and webmail sessions
dek: Web host DreamHost says attackers exploited its File Manager from August to October 23, stealing FTP/SFTP passwords and some webmail sessions.
body:
DreamHost, a long-running web hosting company, has confirmed a breach of the server behind its browser-based File Manager. An attacker exploited a vulnerability there and captured the FTP and SFTP usernames and passwords of customers who logged in to it between about August 2026 and October 23, when the intrusion was found.
The attacker also reached some webmail systems and obtained session information for a limited number of users. A live session can let someone read a mailbox without the password or a second login factor. DreamHost says email contents and files on FTP/SFTP servers may also have been accessed.
## DreamHost's response
DreamHost says well under 10% of customers were affected and found no evidence that control panel logins or billing details were accessed. It reset affected passwords, ended active sessions, rebuilt File Manager with extra security and is offering a year of identity protection. Its notice was filed with California's attorney general on November 2.
## Why site owners should check their files
An FTP login controls the files that make up a website. Even after a password reset, owners should look for files or pages they didn't add.
who: DreamHost customers who used its web File Manager or webmail between August and Oct 23.
todo: Change your FTP, SFTP and email passwords, and check your website files for changes you didn't make.

title: Alation discloses breach exposing Social Security numbers
dek: Enterprise data software company Alation reported a breach to Vermont's attorney general that exposed Social Security numbers and government ID numbers.
body:
Alation, an enterprise software company based in Redwood City, California, has reported a data breach to Vermont's attorney general. The exposed information includes Social Security numbers and government ID numbers.
Alation makes data catalog software used by large companies to organize their data. Its filing doesn't say how many people were affected.
Because Social Security numbers were involved, anyone who gets a notice should consider freezing their credit with the three major bureaus. A freeze is free and blocks new accounts from being opened in your name.
who: People whose records Alation holds, mainly employees and customers' staff.
todo: Watch for a notice and consider freezing your credit, since Social Security numbers were exposed.

title: ISCO International breach exposes Social Security numbers
dek: ISCO International began mailing breach notices on November 2 and reported the incident to the Massachusetts and Vermont attorneys general. SSNs were involved.
body:
ISCO International has disclosed a data breach involving Social Security numbers. The company began mailing notices to affected people on November 2 and reported the incident to the attorneys general of Massachusetts and Vermont.
State filings like these are often the first public sign of a breach. They typically give few details beyond the type of data involved.
Anyone who receives a notice should read it, take up any monitoring it offers and consider a credit freeze, since a stolen Social Security number can be misused years later.
who: People whose records ISCO International holds.
todo: Read your notice and consider a credit freeze, since Social Security numbers were involved.

title: Harvard alumni breach, 851,000 accounts, lands in Have I Been Pwned
dek: Data stolen from Harvard's alumni and donor systems in late 2025 has been added to Have I Been Pwned, so affected people can check their email.
body:
Data from a late-2025 breach of Harvard University's alumni and donor systems has been added to Have I Been Pwned, the free breach-notification service. The dataset covers about 851,000 email addresses.
Adding a breach to the service doesn't mean new data was stolen. It means affected people can now check whether their email address is included, by searching at haveibeenpwned.com.
Alumni and donor records are valuable to scammers because they can support convincing fundraising or "update your details" phishing. Anyone included should change any reused passwords and be cautious with unexpected requests that claim to come from the university.
who: Harvard alumni and donors.
todo: Check your email at haveibeenpwned.com and change any password you reused.

title: Outlook.com and Hotmail start rejecting mail from domains without DMARC
dek: Since November 5, Microsoft's consumer mail services appear to be rejecting some messages from domains with no DMARC record. Small senders should check their DNS.
body:
Email sent to Outlook.com, Hotmail, Live and MSN addresses has started bouncing for some senders. Since about November 5, 2026, Microsoft's consumer mail services appear to be rejecting some messages from domains that have no DMARC record. Microsoft hasn't made a public announcement.
DMARC is a DNS setting that tells receiving mail servers how to handle messages that fail authentication checks. It helps stop scammers from sending mail that pretends to come from your domain. Big providers have been pushing senders to adopt it for years.
## Who should check
Small businesses, clubs and anyone who sends email from their own domain should check that a DMARC record exists. Even a basic monitoring-only policy counts. Your domain or email provider can usually add one in a few minutes.
who: Small businesses and anyone sending email from their own domain to Outlook, Hotmail, Live or MSN addresses.
todo: Ask your email or domain provider to add a DMARC record for your domain.

title: 18 arrested in nine-country crackdown on credit card fraud rings
dek: Police in nine countries, supported by Europol and Eurojust, arrested 18 suspects and carried out 60 house searches in a single day of action against card fraud rings.
body:
Law enforcement agencies in nine countries carried out a coordinated day of action against credit card fraud networks, arresting 18 people and searching 60 homes. Police in Canada, several European countries, Singapore and the United States took part, with support from Europol and Eurojust.
Card fraud rings typically buy stolen card data in bulk, test which cards still work and then cash them out through purchases or money mules.
Arrests like these disrupt the networks, but stolen card data keeps circulating. Checking statements regularly and turning on instant transaction alerts with your bank are still the quickest ways to catch fraud.
who: Victims of credit card fraud and ATM attacks.
todo: Check card statements regularly and turn on transaction alerts with your bank.

title: Europol busts an investment scam network spanning 50 countries
dek: Seven people were arrested and more than 100 servers seized in an action against an investment fraud network that targeted victims in about 50 countries.
body:
On November 3, authorities supported by Europol and Eurojust searched 17 locations, arrested seven people and seized more than 100 servers used by an investment fraud network. One of the raided sites was a call center in Kosovo.
The network targeted victims in around 50 countries. Operations like this usually lure people with fake trading platforms, show them invented profits to encourage bigger deposits, and then make withdrawals impossible.
The safest rule is simple: never invest through someone who contacts you out of the blue, however professional the website looks. Report suspected scams to the police and to your bank right away.
who: People who were cold-called or messaged about online investment opportunities.
todo: Never invest through someone who contacts you out of the blue. Report suspected scams to the police.

title: Google knocks out a 1.3 million-device Android TV box botnet
dek: Google disrupted a botnet of about 1.3 million infected Android TV boxes and says a device maker sold criminals access to them.
body:
Google says it has disrupted a botnet made up of about 1.3 million infected Android TV streaming boxes. It also says a TV box maker sold criminals access to the compromised devices.
Botnets like this are often used to commit ad fraud or to route criminal traffic through ordinary people's home internet connections, which can get their IP addresses flagged or blocked.
Cheap, no-name streaming boxes have been a repeat problem. The safest choice is a device that's Google Play Protect certified from a known brand.
who: Owners of cheap, no-name Android TV streaming boxes.
todo: Replace off-brand streaming boxes with ones that are Google Play Protect certified.

title: FBI seizes the domain of bulletproof host Virtualine
dek: The FBI, working with European police and private partners, seized the domain of Virtualine, a "bulletproof" hosting service accused of serving criminals.
body:
The FBI has seized the website domain of Virtualine, a "bulletproof" hosting provider. Services like it advertise that they ignore abuse complaints and law enforcement requests, which makes them a favorite home for malware, phishing sites and other criminal infrastructure.
Virtualine was also accused of helping launder bitcoin. The seizure was carried out with European police agencies and private-sector partners.
Taking down hosting providers forces criminals to rebuild elsewhere, which costs them time and money. Regular internet users don't need to do anything.
who: Mostly criminals who used the hosting service. Regular users aren't directly affected.
todo: No action needed for most people.

title: Ex-IBM security executive sues IBM and AT&T over alleged hack cover-ups
dek: A former IBM security executive has sued IBM and AT&T, alleging they hid repeated intrusions linked to foreign governments.
body:
A former IBM security executive has filed a lawsuit against IBM and AT&T. It claims the companies concealed repeated network intrusions linked to foreign governments.
The claims are allegations at this stage and haven't been tested in court. If they hold up, they would add to the debate over how and when companies must disclose breaches, an area where U.S. regulators have tightened rules in recent years.
The same news roundup also reported a $400 million fine against South Korean retailer Coupang over its data protection failures.
who: IBM and AT&T customers, and anyone following how companies disclose hacks.
todo: No action needed. Watch for updates as the case moves forward.

title: Citrix patches 12 NetScaler and Secure Access Client flaws, 10 of them critical
dek: Citrix fixed memory bugs in NetScaler ADC and Gateway, an authentication bypass in NetScaler Console, and privilege escalation flaws in its VPN clients. None are known to be exploited yet.
body:
Citrix has released fixes for 12 vulnerabilities across its NetScaler line and its Secure Access Client. Ten carry critical severity scores of 9.3 or higher, according to The Hacker News and SecurityWeek.
## What's affected
Nine of the flaws sit in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway. They are memory-handling bugs that can crash an appliance or make it behave unpredictably. Whether a box is exposed depends on which features are switched on, such as Gateway or AAA virtual servers, DNS load balancing, SMPP or PUSH load balancing, email OTP authentication, Endpoint Analysis or the ICA proxy. One packet-processing flaw, CVE-2026-120868, applies to every ADC and Gateway deployment.
A tenth critical bug, CVE-2026-120869, is an authentication bypass in NetScaler Console that an attacker without credentials could use. The remaining two flaws let a low-privileged user on a Windows or Linux machine running Secure Access Client gain SYSTEM or root rights.
## Why it matters
Citrix says it isn't aware of any exploitation. But NetScaler appliances sit at the network edge and have been a favorite target for years, so attackers often study these patches quickly.
## Fixed versions
- NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1-73.57 and 13.1-64.39 or later, with separate fixed builds for FIPS and NDcPP editions
- NetScaler Console 14.1-74.34 or later
- Secure Access Client 26.11.1.6 for Windows and 26.10.4 for Linux
who: Organizations running NetScaler ADC, NetScaler Gateway or NetScaler Console, and users of Citrix Secure Access Client on Windows or Linux.
todo: Upgrade NetScaler appliances to the fixed builds, starting with internet-facing Gateway and AAA servers, then update NetScaler Console and the Secure Access Client. See Citrix advisories CTX697305, CTX697320, CTX697280 and CTX697281.

title: SignDrop exploit claims a path to SYSTEM on fully patched Windows
dek: A researcher released unpatched proof-of-concept code that abuses the Windows CLFS driver to gain SYSTEM rights. Microsoft hasn't confirmed the flaw, and no attacks have been reported.
body:
A researcher publishing as MSNightmare released a proof-of-concept exploit called SignDrop on the same day Microsoft shipped its November security updates. The researcher says it lets a standard local user on Windows gain SYSTEM privileges, and no patch or CVE exists yet.
## How it works
The exploit targets the Common Log File System driver, clfs.sys. When the driver creates a companion file, the exploit uses object manager symbolic links to redirect it so the file ends up owned by SYSTEM but still writable by the ordinary user. The published code then chains this into a SYSTEM shell, using the Microsoft Defender antimalware service as the privileged process.
The researcher tested it on Windows 11 26H2 and preview builds of Windows Server 2025. The targeted setup is the default one, where a CLFS authentication feature runs in enforcement mode.
## How serious is it
A researcher at PurpleHound confirmed the exploit works but found it too unreliable for real-world use, and Defender must be running for the chain to succeed. It is a local privilege escalation, so an attacker would need a foothold on the machine first. No in-the-wild use has been reported, and the flaw isn't in CISA's catalog of exploited vulnerabilities.
Local privilege escalation bugs are prized by ransomware crews once they get inside a network, so defenders should watch closely for a fix.
who: Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025 systems, especially shared or multi-user machines where an attacker could get a low-privileged foothold.
todo: Watch Microsoft's Security Update Guide for a fix. Don't change the CLFS authentication registry setting to turn the feature off, since that reopens older memory-corruption risks. Keep endpoint detection watching for unusual privilege escalation.

title: PostgreSQL fixes 52 security flaws, including a 22-year-old code execution bug
dek: New PostgreSQL releases fix 52 flaws, led by a type confusion bug that can let a database user run code on the server. Version 14 has now reached end of life.
body:
The PostgreSQL project shipped updates on Nov 12 that fix 52 security vulnerabilities. The fixed releases are 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20 and 14.25.
## The headline bug
The most notable flaw, CVE-2026-6460, is a type confusion bug in composite types rated 8.8. A database user who can create objects may be able to run code on the server as the operating system account that runs PostgreSQL. Its roots trace back to a 2004 change that allowed a column's type to be altered, which is why it is being described as a 22-year-old bug.
Researcher Mehmet Ince published a crash and memory-leak exploit against version 18.6 but held back the final code execution step. He also shared proofs of concept privately with managed database providers.
## Other fixes
- 32 of the 52 flaws are rated 8.8.
- CVE-2026-116322 lets an unauthenticated client restart PostgreSQL 18 servers.
- Several client-tool flaws let a crafted pg_restore archive, or a malicious source server used with pg_dump and psql, run code on the admin's machine.
No attacks have been reported. PostgreSQL 14.25 is the final release for version 14, so anyone still on 14 should plan an upgrade.
who: Anyone running self-managed PostgreSQL servers, plus admins who use pg_dump, pg_restore and psql against databases they don't fully control.
todo: Update to 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20 or 14.25, rebuild C-language extensions at the same time, and restart the server. Update client tools on every machine, follow the reindexing steps in the release notes, and plan a move off PostgreSQL 14.

title: Attackers exploit an UnrealIRCd flaw that hands users server-level commands
dek: CISA says a bug in the popular IRC server software is being exploited. Any user on a linked network could inject commands that run with server authority.
body:
CISA added an UnrealIRCd vulnerability, CVE-2026-114713, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov 13 after reports of attacks. UnrealIRCd is one of the most widely used IRC server packages.
## The flaw
The bug is in the labeled-response module, which fails to escape the IRCv3 label message tag. On a network with two or more linked servers, any connected user can abuse it to inject server-to-server commands. Those commands then run with the authority of a server rather than an ordinary user. It is rated 8.6.
Versions from 6.0.0 up to, but not including, 6.2.7.1 are affected. A hotfix came out on Nov 7, and maintainer Bram Matthys has said exploitation attempts began about a day later. Reports haven't detailed what the attackers were trying to achieve.
## Who needs to act
U.S. federal civilian agencies have until Nov 16 to patch. Anyone else running UnrealIRCd on a linked network should treat this as urgent, since the bug requires nothing more than a connection to the network.
- Fixed in UnrealIRCd 6.2.7.1, or with the hotfix
- If you can't update yet, use the project's spamfilter workaround
IRC is a niche service today, but servers are often run by volunteers with little monitoring, which makes them attractive footholds.
who: Operators of IRC networks that run UnrealIRCd 6 with two or more linked servers.
todo: Upgrade to UnrealIRCd 6.2.7.1 or apply the hotfix now. If that isn't possible, deploy the spamfilter workaround and review server logs for unexpected server-to-server commands.

title: Critical Red Hat Quay flaws expose every private image in a registry
dek: Two critical bugs in Red Hat Quay can let attackers read and overwrite private container images, in one case without an account when anonymous access is on.
body:
Red Hat has disclosed two critical vulnerabilities in Quay, its container image registry, that could give attackers control over private images across an entire registry. Both were found by Red Hat's Dave O'Connor and affect all Quay 3 and Quay 5 versions.
## The two flaws
CVE-2026-123710, rated 9.8, lets an attacker add their own signing key to Quay's list of trusted keys, with no expiry date. Tokens signed with that key grant read and overwrite access to private images in every repository. Because anonymous access is on by default, an attacker may not even need an account. The planted key also survives restarts and password resets.
CVE-2026-110697, rated 9.9, comes from unescaped wildcards in a database search. A user who can create a namespace can steal other tenants' robot account tokens and then read, push or overwrite their images.
## Why it matters
Container registries feed production systems. An attacker who can overwrite images could slip malicious code into software that gets deployed automatically. Red Hat has released fixed builds for several Quay 3 branches, and the hosted Quay.io service is already fixed. There are no reports of exploitation so far.
who: Organizations running self-hosted Red Hat Quay 3 or Quay 5 registries, especially those with anonymous access enabled or many tenants.
todo: Install the fixed Quay release. Until then, block the /keys endpoint at the proxy except for trusted internal components, search audit logs for service key events with no expiration date, remove unknown keys, and rotate robot tokens.

title: Attackers exploit N-central flaws to plant cryptominers, even on patched servers
dek: Researchers found Monero miners on 21 N-able N-central servers within hours of exploit code going public. Nineteen were already running the latest hotfix.
body:
Attackers began exploiting newly disclosed flaws in N-able's N-central remote management platform within hours of proof-of-concept code being published, according to SecurityWeek and The Hacker News. The flaws were among a batch disclosed by independent researcher Sean Bales.
## What happened
Security firm Huntback found the XMRig Monero miner on 21 N-central servers, and 19 of them were already running Hotfix 2. The miner was set to use only half of the CPU cores, likely to avoid notice. Previdian also reported the attacks, and N-able later confirmed the targeting and shared indicators of compromise.
One chain, dubbed 4EverAble2Shell, combines a critical Apache Axis flaw, CVE-2026-90436, with an N-central privilege escalation weakness to gain root. A second set, Agent2Shell, can lead to code execution as root and SYSTEM-level access on Windows under certain conditions.
## N-able's response
N-able is restricting some features and integrations. On hosted environments, the Legacy API is now off by default and Intune integration is disabled. The company says attackers are going after customers who haven't disabled the Legacy API.
Because N-central manages fleets of client machines, a compromised server can be a gateway to many downstream networks. A cryptominer today could be something worse tomorrow.
who: Managed service providers and IT teams running N-able N-central, hosted or on premises.
todo: Upgrade Agents and Probes as N-able directs, confirm the Legacy API is disabled on premises, and hunt for the published indicators, including the 157.20.241.16 address and the jup.sh script. Treat any hit as a full compromise; Hotfix 2 alone isn't enough.

title: Hackers chain PHP2Shell bugs to backdoor Check Point gateways and wipe servers
dek: Check Point says attackers broke into unpatched gateways, planted a backdoor and in some cases destroyed VMware ESXi hosts. CISA has added a related flaw to its exploited list.
body:
Check Point has detailed a campaign that began on Oct 30 in which attackers exploited PHP2Shell flaws in its security gateways and management servers, then escalated privileges with a separate bug, CVE-2026-123039. CISA added that flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov 13.
## The attack chain
Attackers used PHP2Shell for initial access and CVE-2026-123039, a missing authorization flaw rated 7.8, to become root. They then installed PHP web shells and a backdoor called TSGA, disguised as a Check Point process, along with a networking component called TSProxy. From there they scanned the network, moved over SSH to VMware ESXi hosts and ran a wiper that deletes files regardless of type.
## Victims
The first wave on Oct 30 hit Israeli organizations, some of which suffered destructive wiping. A second wave on Nov 2 was opportunistic and hit organizations in several countries and sectors. Check Point says a couple of dozen customers were affected.
## Who is behind it
TSGA and TSProxy belong to a toolkit that ESET previously linked to a China-nexus group. Check Point says it doesn't have enough evidence to tie this campaign to that group and is weighing other explanations, including a false flag. A fix was available about a week before the first wave.
who: Organizations running Check Point firewalls, management and log servers, Multi-Domain servers or Maestro Orchestrator on versions R81 through R82.20.
todo: Apply Check Point's fix (SK1000362) now if you haven't. Look for unknown PHP files, unfamiliar processes posing as Check Point services, and unusual SSH connections from gateways to ESXi hosts. U.S. federal agencies must patch by Nov 16.

title: SilentAir spies hijack Asian telecom gear to intercept calls and 2FA texts
dek: Researchers say a state-level group compromised equipment inside mobile operators to divert calls and texts, mostly targeting Taiwanese officials and VIPs.
body:
Telecom security firm Enea has exposed a group it calls SilentAir that broke into equipment inside Asian mobile operators and used it to intercept phone calls and text messages. Enea assesses with high confidence that it is a state-level actor, but links the activity to China only with low confidence.
## How it worked
The attackers used the hacked equipment to send signaling messages across the network that connects mobile carriers worldwide. Those messages falsely claimed the compromised equipment was now serving a target's phone, so the target's calls and texts were rerouted to the attackers. Enea also saw large numbers of silent SMS messages, which appear to have been used to check whether the diversions were still working.
For some targets, two-factor authentication codes were intercepted right after a diversion, suggesting attempts to break into other accounts. Enea did not say whether any account was taken over.
## Who was targeted
Most targets were in Taiwan, including political and government figures. Others were in Southeast and East Asia, with occasional targets in East Africa, Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. Activity came in month-long bursts separated by long gaps, and Enea has tracked it since early 2025. The firm says the operation has been disrupted for now but could return.
who: Mobile operators in Asia and their customers, especially government officials and other high-value people in Taiwan who rely on SMS codes.
todo: Operators should treat inter-carrier signaling traffic as untrusted and deploy signaling firewalls. High-risk users should switch from SMS codes to authenticator apps or security keys.

title: FBI says North Korean hackers stole $400 million using fake video calls
dek: A scheme the FBI calls FaceStealer used hijacked accounts, recorded or deepfaked video and fake audio errors to trick crypto executives and developers into installing malware.
body:
The FBI says North Korea-linked hackers stole more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over roughly 18 months through a social engineering scheme it calls FaceStealer. U.S. authorities seized the cloud infrastructure behind it and more than 900 webcam recordings of victims.
## How the scam works
Attackers send meeting invitations, often over Telegram, from accounts they hijacked from earlier victims. On the call, the target sees prerecorded video of a trusted contact or a deepfake of a well-known industry figure, while their own webcam is secretly recorded. A fake audio problem then prompts the victim to click a link or run a command to fix it, which installs malware. Lookalike Zoom and Teams domains are part of the setup. Each new victim's account is then used to approach their contacts.
## Who is behind it
The activity is tied to BlueNoroff, a financially motivated North Korean cluster also tracked as APT38 and Sapphire Sleet. Researchers have counted hundreds of targets across dozens of countries, most of them founders and executives in crypto and Web3, as well as open-source developers. The FBI warned the group is also going after developers of widely used software libraries.
The same day, the Justice Department announced it had seized or restrained more than $1.2 billion stolen in the Binance hack.
who: Cryptocurrency and Web3 founders, executives and investors, plus open-source maintainers and developers who take meetings with people they don't know well.
todo: Never run commands or install software to fix a call's audio or video. Verify meeting invites through a separate channel, even from known contacts, and open job tests or downloads only in a disposable virtual machine.

title: wfx-loot campaign hits tens of thousands of GitHub repos to steal CI secrets
dek: An attacker using stolen GitHub accounts probed more than 61,000 repositories and ran a secret-stealing script in over 1,800 of them, then used the loot to break into cloud accounts.
body:
Security firm Aikido has uncovered a campaign it calls wfx-loot that uses stolen GitHub credentials to steal secrets from continuous integration pipelines. Activity began on Nov 10.
## The scale
Aikido counted 4,837 compromised accounts that opened probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories. The malicious script actually ran in more than 1,800 of them. More than 10,000 of the probes landed in repositories the compromised accounts didn't own but could reach through collaborator or organization access. SecurityWeek separately reported the campaign targeting about 60,000 repositories.
## How it works
The attacker first opens a harmless-looking pull request about dependency audit notes to test for write access. It then pushes a long shell script through an existing workflow, an npm install hook or a new workflow, and within about a minute reverts the change and deletes the run logs.
The script grabs GitHub Actions secrets, cloud and SSH credentials, shell histories and AI tool tokens. Aikido saw the attacker use them to get into AWS, Google Cloud and Azure, create long-lived AWS keys, loosen an AWS role's trust policy and forge passing status checks. Automated publishing also pushed the payload into a Packagist package and two Go module tags.
Aikido says this is likely a different actor from October's GhostAction campaign.
who: Developers and organizations using GitHub Actions, especially maintainers who publish packages to npm, PyPI, Packagist, Go or crates.
todo: Search your repos for a wfx-docs branch, a probe pull request titled docs: dependency audit notes, and commits titled ci: refresh build cache or chore: add ci helper. If the script ran, rotate every reachable secret and undo any AWS trust policy or Azure federated credential changes.

title: Spies used an open-source AI pentest tool to break into 10 organizations
dek: Unit 42 says a likely China-nexus operator let an AI framework called Cairn run intrusions against semiconductor, defense and civil society targets, and no model refused.
body:
Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 says a likely China-nexus espionage operator used a customized fork of Cairn, an open-source AI penetration testing framework, to carry out intrusions in August and September. Unit 42 tracks the activity as CL-STA-1238 and makes the China link with moderate confidence.
## What happened
Cairn hands an intrusion to an AI model, which repeatedly chooses and runs the next step. The operator ran 25 operations against at least 19 organizations and got unauthorized access or stole data at 10 of them. Operations lasted anywhere from about 20 minutes to more than 50 hours.
Results included valid credentials and an altered ballot document at an industry standards body, access to more than a million member records at a U.S. teachers' union, new admin accounts at a semiconductor company, and user records with military and government addresses from a defense-policy program.
## The AI angle
The operator used Zhipu and DeepSeek models. None refused, because the tasks were framed as authorized testing backed by generated authorization files.
## What it means
Unit 42 says the AI raised the volume and reach of the attacks, not their sophistication. Most of the holes exploited were familiar ones: authentication bypasses, weak or default passwords, exposed cloud APIs and old public CVEs.
who: Semiconductor and advanced manufacturing suppliers, defense and policy groups, and human rights and civil society organizations.
todo: Cover the basics that AI-driven attacks exploit: remove default and weak passwords, enforce MFA, shrink exposed services and patch old CVEs. Check logs for the published indicators 154.44.31[.]4 and 82.29.129[.]54.

title: Fake Teams meeting bookings trick victims into approving attacker logins
dek: Huntress found a phishing kit that disguises a Microsoft device sign-in code as a booking reference, so victims approve the attacker's session on Microsoft's real login page.
body:
Huntress has described a device code phishing attack dressed up as a Microsoft Teams meeting booking, Help Net Security reports. The target was an employee at a construction company.
## How the trick works
Microsoft's device code sign-in lets you log in on one device by typing a short code on another. The attacker starts such a sign-in, receives a code, and shows it to the victim on a lure page labeled as a booking reference. When the victim enters that code on Microsoft's genuine login page, they unknowingly approve the attacker's session. The attacker then gets valid tokens for the victim's account.
The lure arrived by email from a lookalike domain impersonating a senior vice president at another construction firm, with a Google share link that redirected to the lure page.
## Built to evade
- The phishing page was encrypted and decrypted itself in the browser, which defeats scanners that don't run JavaScript.
- If Microsoft returned an error, the kit quietly started a fresh device code session.
- The final login came through a residential proxy to look like ordinary home traffic.
Because the victim signs in on the real Microsoft page, the usual advice to check the web address doesn't help here. The safer habit is to never enter a sign-in code you didn't request yourself.
who: Microsoft 365 users, particularly in industries like construction where meetings with outside contacts are routine.
todo: Be suspicious of any request to enter a code on Microsoft's device login page that you didn't start. Admins should block or limit device code sign-in with conditional access where it isn't needed and use phishing-resistant MFA.

title: Trezor finds hidden spy boards in wallets sold by a Southeast Asian reseller
dek: Three Trezor Safe 5 wallets bought from reseller CryptoBilis had an extra circuit board that copies recovery phrases and sends them out over the mobile network.
body:
Hardware wallet maker Trezor has confirmed that three Trezor Safe 5 devices bought from CryptoBilis, a former official reseller in Southeast Asia, contained a hidden circuit board built to steal recovery phrases.
## How the implant works
The board sits between the wallet's main board and its screen. It captures the recovery phrase when the wallet displays it during backup or when a user types it in to restore a wallet, and it grabs any passphrase too. It then encrypts the data and sends it over the mobile network to an attacker's server, retrying until it succeeds. It doesn't touch the wallet's firmware or secure chip, which is why normal integrity checks wouldn't catch it.
## Scope
The three devices were bought between Aug 20 and Sept 23 through CryptoBilis stores on Tokopedia and Shopee. Trezor removed the reseller on Oct 9 and says 48 people have contacted it so far. No losses have been reported. Trezor says the implants resemble those Ledger found in devices from the same reseller. Who installed them, and where in the supply chain, is still unknown.
Firmware 2.13.1 blocks the known implants, but it can't protect a phrase that was already captured. Trezor has also cut its reseller network by about 80%.
who: Anyone who bought a Trezor or other hardware wallet from CryptoBilis, or through its Tokopedia or Shopee shops, since March 2026.
todo: If you bought from CryptoBilis, move funds to a new wallet with a brand-new recovery phrase and contact Trezor Support for a replacement. Buy hardware wallets directly from the maker, and never share your recovery phrase.

title: Maersk investigates breach of a legacy system as WhiteArmor demands $5 million
dek: The shipping giant says an old system from a past acquisition was accessed but operations aren't affected. The WhiteArmor gang claims 100GB of data and wants $5 million.
body:
A.P. Moller-Maersk is investigating a potential ransomware attack involving unauthorized access to a legacy system it inherited from an earlier acquisition. The WhiteArmor data extortion and ransomware group claimed responsibility on Nov 8.
## What Maersk says
Maersk said that, based on its findings so far, no sensitive data has been stolen. It says the incident is contained to that local system, doesn't affect its other systems or the partner systems that connect to it, and isn't expected to disrupt operations. Customers can keep booking and managing shipments.
## What the attackers claim
WhiteArmor says it holds about 100GB of data, including driver records, staff accounts, delivery recipients' names and addresses, and mobile device logs. It is demanding $5 million in bitcoin within 30 days and threatening to publish the files otherwise. The group told ISMG that Maersk hasn't contacted it. None of these claims have been independently verified.
WhiteArmor appeared in late October and says it has hit more than 20 organizations.
## Why it stands out
Maersk was one of the biggest victims of the 2017 NotPetya attack, which shut down its network for about 10 days. This incident looks far smaller, but it shows how forgotten systems picked up in acquisitions can become an entry point.
who: Maersk, plus drivers, staff and delivery recipients whose details may have been in the affected legacy system.
todo: If you deal with Maersk, watch for phishing that references shipments or deliveries. Organizations should inventory, patch or isolate legacy systems inherited through acquisitions.

title: UT Arlington warns of stolen data after Qilin claims the attack
dek: The University of Texas at Arlington says hackers stole personal information in an October breach. The Qilin ransomware gang has claimed responsibility.
body:
The University of Texas at Arlington has warned students and employees that personal information was stolen in a cybersecurity incident last month, The Record reports. The Qilin ransomware gang claimed the attack the same week.
## What the university has said
The university says an investigation confirmed that data was taken, but it hasn't said what kinds of information were involved or how many people are affected. It is still working out whose data was taken and plans to contact those people directly.
When the attack was first announced, the university took its MachForms portal offline. That system handles event registrations, service requests and surveys, and it remained offline at the time of the report.
## About Qilin
Qilin has become one of the most active ransomware operations. Data from Halcyon cited by The Record puts it at 344 alleged attacks between July and September, the second-highest of any group. It recently claimed an attack on the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.
## A pattern in higher education
Universities hold large amounts of sensitive data on students, staff and alumni, and they have been frequent ransomware targets this year. Earlier this month Vanderbilt University was hit by a different gang.
who: UT Arlington students, employees and others who used the university's MachForms portal.
todo: Watch for a notification from UT Arlington, be wary of phishing that mentions the university, and consider a credit freeze if you're told your Social Security number was involved.

title: BlackNevas ransomware wiped an entire VMware estate without exploiting a bug
dek: Kaspersky says the attackers used stolen credentials and normal VMware admin tools to destroy four ESXi hosts, every VM and the backups over 10 days.
body:
Kaspersky's incident response team has detailed a BlackNevas ransomware attack that destroyed an organization's whole virtualization environment over 10 days. The attackers wiped four VMware ESXi hosts, every virtual machine on them, both vCenter appliances and the connected backup infrastructure. BlackNevas is linked to the Trigona ransomware family.
## No exploit needed
The attackers didn't use any hypervisor vulnerability. They started with credentials stolen from other systems, which got them into vCenter. On the disaster recovery vCenter, they logged in as root over SSH, installed remote access and tunneling tools, and disguised one of them as a VMware service.
They then abused vCenter's Host Profiles compliance feature to switch on SSH across the ESXi hosts and connected from the trusted vCenter address. To most monitoring, it looked like routine administration.
## Backups went first
Days before the final blow, the attackers disabled antivirus in the backup environment, stopped backup services and encrypted the recovery repositories. When the destructive payload finally ran, virtual machines stopped within 23 seconds and the start of each virtual disk was overwritten, leaving nothing to boot.
The victim's name, sector and location weren't disclosed. The lesson for defenders is that vCenter deserves the same protection as a domain controller.
who: Organizations running VMware vSphere, vCenter and ESXi, especially where vCenter shares credentials or identity with Active Directory.
todo: Treat vCenter as a top-tier asset with dedicated admin accounts and phishing-resistant MFA. Send ESXi and vCenter logs to remote syslog, alert on Host Profile changes that enable SSH, separate backup credentials from production AD, and test restores without vCenter.

title: Ransomware knocks Belarusian cloud host ActiveCloud offline for days
dek: An attack encrypted parts of ActiveCloud's infrastructure, taking down websites, email and virtual servers for businesses in Belarus and Russia.
body:
ActiveCloud, a provider of cloud hosting, virtual servers and corporate email for businesses in Belarus and Russia, was hit by a ransomware attack that disrupted customers for several days, The Record reports. The company disclosed the attack on Nov 10.
## Impact
Hackers broke into ActiveCloud's systems and encrypted parts of its cloud infrastructure. Corporate websites, email, virtual servers, cloud hosting and customer support channels were all affected, including its E-Cloud and SmartMail products. Local news outlet Smartpress said its website ran on ActiveCloud's infrastructure, and Domino's Pizza in Belarus had temporary outages to its site and app.
Key infrastructure came back by Wednesday and main services by Friday, though some customers were still struggling to restore virtual machines. ActiveCloud said its investigation found no evidence that customer data was stolen.
## Unknowns
No ransomware group has been named, and ActiveCloud hasn't explained how the attackers got in. The Record notes recent attacks on Russian hosting providers ESTT and Beget, but there's no public evidence linking them.
## Why it matters
Attacks on hosting providers spread the damage widely. One breach can take down many businesses that never had direct contact with the attackers.
who: ActiveCloud customers in Belarus and Russia and the businesses that rely on their websites, email and virtual servers.
todo: Customers should verify restored virtual machines and data, change passwords for hosting accounts, and keep independent backups outside their hosting provider.

title: Stolen Fireworks AI key led to a Cursor breach and a trojanized extension
dek: Cursor says an access key exposed in a Fireworks AI breach let an attacker copy shared data and later push a backdoored Claude Code extension to up to 5,000 users.
body:
Cursor, the AI coding editor, has explained how a recent attack on its systems began. An access key it had issued to AI inference provider Fireworks AI was exposed when Fireworks itself was breached.
## What the attacker did
Using that key, the attacker copied data from a read-only storage bucket that Cursor used to share data with Fireworks. Credentials found in that data led the attacker into some of Cursor's software-as-a-service tools. Later, using a stolen credential, the attacker placed a trojanized build of Anthropic's Claude Code extension on the cache behind Cursor's extension marketplace on Oct 29. It was delivered as a normal update, tried to install a persistent SSH backdoor and stayed up for about 11 hours.
## What was exposed
- Archived non-production source code repositories
- Some support emails, usage metrics and contact details
- Summaries of some coding agent conversations
- Credentials some users had sent to support, and API credentials found in agent traces for fewer than 0.01% of customers
Cursor says Privacy Mode users, customer code repositories, its production environment and the Cursor app itself weren't affected. At most 5,000 users may have received the malicious extension.
## The bigger picture
Uber and Notion have also disclosed data theft tied to the Fireworks breach, showing how one AI vendor can become a doorway into its customers.
who: Cursor users who installed Claude Code extension versions 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 on Oct 29, users who shared credentials with Cursor support, and other Fireworks AI customers.
todo: If you installed the affected extension versions, treat the machine as compromised and rotate any credentials on it. Rotate API keys you've pasted into support chats or agent sessions, and review which AI vendors hold keys to your data.

title: Expedia confirms breach through a data vendor as extortion gang claims huge haul
dek: Expedia says attackers reached its systems via a compromised third-party data platform. A new group called n0n claims hundreds of millions of records, which Expedia hasn't confirmed.
body:
